newsitem.title: UK: Russia upgrade prospects seen slim, outlook rosier.
newsitem.headline: Russia upgrade prospects seen slim, outlook rosier.

text.p: Russia's chances of getting a sovereign credit upgrade this year are slim, although economic and fiscal improvements probably warrant a more favourable ratings outlook, analysts said on Monday.
Major rating agencies are due to assess Russia's situation this year, in an annual review which is routine practice for sovereign credits.
Russia's newly established presence in the Eurobond market as a regional benchmark borrower has focused investor attention on its ratings prospects.
"There is a very low chance of an upgrade, especially after one year," one economist familiar with Russia's rating process said.
"One should not assume that Russia will get an upgrade this year," the economist said, adding progress made in the last year could lead to a change in Russia's rating outlook to positive from stable.

Last October Moody's Investors Service gave Russia's long-term foreign currency debt a Ba2 rating. Standard & Poor's Corp assigned it a BB minus rating, with a stable outlook, and IBCA a BB plus level.
None is investment grade, the minimum level at which many institutional investors can buy debt, but were better than expected at the time.

S&P said in July it would assess Russia in the near future, but could not specify a date. It is standard practice for the major agencies not to comment on credit standings outside of official announcements.

"Both rating agencies (Moody's and S&P) will be returning to Russia some time between September and December and doing a review," Daniel McGovern, head of emerging market research at Merrill Lynch in London said.
"The question of an upgrade is somewhat contingent upon events within Russia, particularly the ability of the government in October to pass key pieces of legislation in the Duma (parliament)."
Analysts said both rating agencies had come under intense scrutiny when Russia's ratings were assigned, and had indicated the levels given were "durable".
Some other Eastern European countries, like Poland and the Czech Republic, did receive quick rating rises, but bankers said this was because the agencies had been too cautious in the first place.

"Rating agencies don't really upgrade a country every year. When they rated some of the Eastern European transition economies it was difficult to put a credit risk profile to the countries and they had to correct their initial perception," the economist said.
"This was not the case with Russia. There was a lot of due diligence done. The initial rating was very carefully considered so we would not expect that to be changed this year," the economist added.
Last April Polish long-term foreign currency debt was upgraded to BBB minus by S&P, from BB. Then in June of 1997, S&P changed the outlook to positive from stable.
Poland already had a Baa3 investment grade rating from Moody's, awarded in 1995, and analysts expect it to rece the single-A level.
The Czech Republic is rated A by S&P, upped in November 1995 from BBB plus.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin installed a new reformist cabinet in March, and since then pension arrears have been paid and inflation and interest rates have come down in Russia.
Among problems still facing Russia is a web of unpaid bills between companies and the state, which nearly doubled to 27 percent of gross domestic product over the first half of the year.
"The budget and revisions in the budget, which include cuts in spending and some tax increases, will be put before the Duma in October," McGovern said.

"The rating agencies will look to see progress on those specific events before they approve an upgrade. One or more of the rating agencies may put a positive outlook on Russia, but it may be a bit early for an upgrade."
Since receiving its ratings, Russia has successfully tapped the international capital markets. Last November it launched its first bond since the 1917 revolution -- a $1.0 billion five-year Eurobond.

Barely six months later, in June, it raised $2.0 billion via a 10-year bond. Bankers said the doubling of both size and maturity in such a short period indicated improved investor sentiment towards the country.
